findings.headline: Building Control cost-recovery monitoring process not started as of early September, with October completion target one month away
findings.detail: Auditors recommended formalizing a three-year rolling cost-recovery review to determine whether Building Control aligns fee levels to the full-cost-recovery principle. As of early September, work had not been started; the responsible officer is only 'proposing' to engage Finance to complete it. Target completion is October 2026.
findings.matters: Auditor recommendation for formal cost-recovery monitoring suggests questions about whether the service currently self-finances or requires general-fund subsidy. A finance director needs visibility of which services run at cost and which are subsidized.
findings.figures: No current figures provided; three-year rolling monitoring framework to be established
findings.quote: Liaison to occur with BDBC Finance to introduce a documented three-year rolling cost recovery review to monitor cumulative surpluses or deficits and ensure fee levels remain aligned to the full-cost recovery principle

findings.headline: Standby generator installation at Wade Road deferred from 2026 to 2027-28, postponing critical business continuity infrastructure
findings.detail: Installation of a standby generator at Wade Road, marked Significant risk, has been deferred to next financial year (2027-28) pending planning permission and IT coordination. Initially flagged as requiring 'upmost priority', installation is now postponed by approximately one year.
findings.matters: Deferral of flagged-priority business continuity infrastructure indicates capital constraints or shifting risk priorities. The facility operates without adequate backup power until 2028.
findings.figures: No cost disclosed
findings.quote: The installation of a stand-by generator, integrated with the UPS at Wade Road should be given the upmost priority

findings.headline: Waste and Recycling Services contract indexation position unresolved in September, disputed invoices to be reviewed once rates are settled
findings.detail: An unresolved commercial dispute exists over contract indexation and billing rates with the council's waste contractor. Variable invoices and credit notes require review and adjustment once the indexation position is resolved, including restatement of default amounts previously billed. As of early September the matter remained 'Ongoing. Subject to negotiation' with a December 2026 target, marked COMMERCIAL IN CONFIDENCE.
findings.matters: Unresolved contractual disputes represent financial uncertainty and potential liability for disputed invoicing. The scope and direction of any billing adjustment remain unknown.
findings.figures: Supporting values marked COMMERCIAL IN CONFIDENCE; documented as 'values excluding and including indexation'
findings.quote: Once the indexation position has been resolved, variable credit notes/invoices issued should be reviewed in detail to ensure they reflect correct contract rates

findings.headline: Treasury portfolio outperforming peer benchmarks on returns with lower credit risk
findings.detail: In benchmarking against 226 council participants, Basingstoke's treasury portfolio achieved weighted average return of 4.15% against benchmark average of 3.93%, while holding significantly lower credit risk (1.00 vs 1.76). The council has also lengthened investment maturities to 289 days average vs 52 days for peers, locking in fixed rates and providing income certainty.
findings.matters: Demonstrates effective treasury management generating superior returns while managing risk prudently, indicating capable finance leadership.
findings.figures: Return 4.15% vs benchmark 3.93%; credit risk indicator 1.00 vs benchmark 1.76; maturity 289 days vs 52 days
findings.quote: The average return being achieved by the council is above the benchmark average. The average maturity indicates that the council has fixed many of its interest rates for a longer period than the benchmark average and this provides the council with a greater certainty of its future investment income. The council also holds investments with much lower credit risk than the average.

findings.headline: Council approves expanded lending to future merger partners Rushmoor and Hart ahead of April 2028 reorganisation
findings.detail: On 16 July 2026, the council approved amendments to the Treasury Management Strategy allowing loans to Rushmoor Borough Council and Hart District Council to exceed the standard £10M individual counterparty limit. These councils are expected to merge with Basingstoke and Deane on 1 April 2028 as part of the proposed Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Signals structural change to the council's operating model with major governance transition planned for April 2028, creating potential risks and opportunities for merged entity's financial management.
findings.figures: Individual counterparty limit raised beyond £10M for Rushmoor and Hart; merger date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: It is expected that these councils will merge with Basingstoke and Deane Borough Council on 1st April 2028 as part of the proposed Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Externally managed funds showing unrealised losses of £2.27M against cost
findings.detail: The council's pooled investments in bond and property funds are valued at £22.73M on 30 June 2026 against a cost of £25.00M, representing unrealised losses of £2.27M. A statutory accounting override allows these losses to be held off the P&L account until 1 April 2029. During Q1 2026/27, fund valuations improved by £0.09M.
findings.matters: Represents potential future losses in the investment portfolio and valuation risk. While statutory protections prevent current P&L impact, the council holds material unrealised losses that could crystallise at disposal.
findings.figures: Fund valuation £22.73M vs cost £25.00M (loss £2.27M); Q1 improvement £0.09M
findings.quote: On 30 June 2026 the valuation of the council's externally managed funds was £22.73M compared to an initial cost of £25.00M, therefore showing a reduction of £2.27M.

findings.headline: Base rate held at 3.75% contrary to MTFS assumption of reduction to 3.25% by end 2026
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27 to 2029/30 assumed the Bank of England base rate would fall from 3.75% to 3.25% by end 2026. In reality, the base rate has remained at 3.75% throughout the financial year. The report indicates further rate stability or increases are likely due to oil price pressures and supply chain disruption.
findings.matters: Divergence of actual rates from strategic assumptions affects forward budget planning and revenue projections, with implications for the council's financial position across the MTFS period.
findings.figures: Base rate: 3.75% actual vs 3.25% MTFS assumption; CPI fell from 3.3% to 2.6%
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2029/30 assumed that the base rate would be reduced from 3.75% to 3.25% by the end of 2026 and would remain at this level through the remainder of the MTFS period.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income forecast at £5.06M, £0.65M above budget
findings.detail: Net interest and investment income for 2026/27 forecast at £5.06M against budget of £4.41M, outperforming by 15%. Outperformance driven by new long-term loans arranged after budget setting and liquidity cash returns exceeding forecast as base rates remain higher than originally assumed.
findings.matters: Additional investment income of £0.65M improves the council's financial position and demonstrates effective cash management, with implications for future resource availability.
findings.figures: Net income forecast £5.06M vs budget £4.41M (£0.65M above); overall return 4.12% vs budget 3.80%
findings.quote: Net income for the year is forecast to be £0.65M above the budget estimate total of £4.41M in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Formal firewall governance policy remains in draft form past its August 2026 deadline.
findings.detail: A formal firewall policy covering rule creation, approval processes, change control, ownership documentation and other governance areas was due in August 2026. As of 1 September 2026, the policy document was still in draft form being jointly developed by Infrastructure and Cyber teams.
findings.matters: Formal firewall governance is a material cybersecurity control; operating without it increases operational risk and suggests the council's IT control environment is incomplete.
findings.figures: Target date August 2026; draft status as of 01/09/2026
findings.quote: The firewall Fortinet 200F processes and management document is in draft form.

findings.headline: Master list of the council's cloud and processing systems remains incomplete and status is now unclear.
findings.detail: Originally due June 2025, the deadline was revised to June 2026 as part of a broader information asset register to be completed in 2026-2027. As of 10 September 2026, the most recent comment states the status is uncertain and requires follow-up.
findings.matters: A council that cannot produce a master inventory of its information systems and processing lacks a fundamental data governance control; this is a baseline security and compliance requirement.
findings.figures: Audit completion March 2025; revised target June 2026; current status uncertain as at 10/09/2026
findings.quote: 10/09/26 - Now unsure, need to follow up.

findings.headline: Partnership SLA remains unsigned 16 months after its original target date.
findings.detail: The service level agreement between BDBC and HCC for the Manydown Major Strategic Partnership was due for signature by July 2025. As of June 2026, amendments had been agreed and the agreement was reported as 'just needs to be signed', but the September 2026 update shows no progress: 'No update received'.
findings.matters: Manydown is a major capital scheme requiring formal partnership governance; an unsigned SLA between the council and its partner leaves the partnership framework incomplete and governance exposure unmanaged.
findings.figures: Audit completion March 2025; original target date July 2025; most recent update 09/09/2026
findings.quote: Just needs to be signed. Will send IAM a copy when signed. 09/0/9/26 - No update received.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 01072026 1830 Audit and Accounts Committee
findings.headline: Number of overdue internal audit recommendations has decreased.
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Manager reported that the number of overdue audit recommendations had reduced following work undertaken by Internal Audit with teams within the Council, indicating increased responsiveness to audit findings.
findings.matters: Timely implementation of audit recommendations is a key governance strength; reducing overdue items demonstrates the council is addressing control weaknesses identified by auditors.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: It was highlighted that the number of overdue audit recommendations had reduced following work undertaken by Internal Audit with teams within the Council.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 01072026 1830 Audit and Accounts Committee
findings.headline: Audit risk on Manydown Garden Communities LLP group accounting has decreased from prior year.
findings.detail: In the prior year, the first year of group accounts preparation, there was elevated audit risk related to group accounting for this joint venture. External auditors have now confirmed the audit risk level has decreased, indicating the council has established effective processes for managing this complex accounting area.
findings.matters: Group accounting for joint ventures is a complex audit area; decreased audit risk demonstrates sound controls have been established, which is important to lenders assessing governance quality.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: the level of audit risk related to the group accounting for the Manydown Garden Communities LLP joint venture had decreased.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 01072026 1830 Audit and Accounts Committee
findings.headline: Treasury strategy to be amended to increase flexibility in local authority lending limits to Hart and Rushmoor in context of LGR.
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer proposed changes to the Treasury Management Strategy to increase flexibility in local authority loan lending limits to Hart District Council and Rushmoor Borough Council considering Local Government Reorganisation proposals. The council has already provided a loan to Rushmoor under the existing strategy. The CFO advised that the proposed change could reduce future borrowing costs for the new authority.
findings.matters: Strategic treasury changes ahead of reorganisation with expected reduction in future borrowing costs directly affect the council's financial position and liquidity planning.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: proposed changes to the strategy to be presented to Council for approval, including greater flexibility within the local authority loan lending limit to Hart District Council and Rushmoor Borough Council considering Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) proposals.

findings.headline: Total reserves reduced by £0.2M net following audit adjustments.
findings.detail: Corrections to the appeals provision and Safety Net calculation resulted in usable reserves falling £0.2M and unusable reserves rising £0.5M, reducing total reserves by £0.2M. Reflects tighter financial buffers after audit identified prior estimation errors.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's buffer for unexpected demands or revenue volatility. Any reduction in reserve headroom is relevant to lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Usable reserves down £0.2M, unusable reserves up £0.5M, net reduction in total reserves £0.2M
findings.quote: The overall impact of the above adjustments is a reduction in usable reserves of £0.2M and an increase in unusable reserves of £0.5M. A net reduction in total reserves of £0.2M.

findings.headline: Business rates income revised down £0.2M due to formula error in appeals provision.
findings.detail: Audit identified a formula error that had understated the appeals provision by £1.2M (£0.5M affecting Basingstoke). Partially offset by a £0.3M adjustment to the Safety Net calculation. Net result: retained business rates income reduced from £4.9M to £4.7M.
findings.matters: Business rates are a significant council revenue stream. Downward revisions and audit corrections to material items indicate estimation or control issues affecting financial forecasting reliability.
findings.figures: Appeals provision understated £1.2M (£0.5M to council), Safety Net adjustment +£0.3M, retained business rates reduced from £4.9M to £4.7M
findings.quote: due to a formula error, the appeals provision had been understated by £1.2M of which 40% is the Basingstoke element of £0.5M

findings.headline: Audit qualification scope narrowing after disclaimed opinions in 2022/23 and 2023/24.
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed audits (no opinion) for 2022/23 and 2023/24 due to inability to verify opening balances. In 2024/25, EY issued a qualified opinion as it rebuilt evidence. For 2025/26, a qualified opinion is expected but with 'more limited in scope', showing continuing progress toward clean audit opinions.
findings.matters: A lender needs reliable auditor verification. Movement from disclaimed to qualified to narrowing-scope-qualified shows the council is rebuilding financial controls and systems, reducing audit risk.
findings.figures: 2022/23 disclaimed; 2023/24 disclaimed; 2024/25 qualified; 2025/26 qualified (scope narrowing)
findings.quote: the basis for the qualification will be more limited in scope reflecting the progress made on building back assurance

findings.headline: Sundry Debtors audit upgraded to Full Assurance following significant improvements to debt recovery
findings.detail: The Sundry Debtors function improved from Substantial Assurance in 2025/26 to Full Assurance in 2026/27. The report notes 'significant improvements have been made to sundry debt recovery arrangements, with regular monitoring and recovery activity now in place', reversing previous audit findings that had been 'more challenging'.
findings.matters: Improved debt recovery directly strengthens cash position and collection rates; this audit upgrade shows the council has successfully remediated previously identified weaknesses in a core financial control.
findings.figures: Upgrade from Substantial Assurance (2025/26) to Full Assurance (2026/27)
findings.quote: Significant improvements have been made to sundry debt recovery arrangements, with regular monitoring and recovery activity now in place.

findings.headline: Building Control cannot demonstrate cost recovery despite being a fee-funded service
findings.detail: Audit of Building Control identified that management has 'limited evidence of formal three-year cost recovery monitoring' and 'an absence of recent statutory financial statements'. Charge rates are not being implemented on time. These failures mean the council cannot confirm whether the service is genuinely cost-neutral or is being subsidised from general funds.
findings.matters: A fee-funded service without cost recovery monitoring creates an unquantified fiscal risk; the council may be unknowingly subsidising the service or leaving capacity unutilised, either of which affects financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 28,000 open online legacy records requiring digitisation
findings.quote: Financial management arrangements require strengthening to support regulatory compliance and long-term sustainability. The audit identified issues relating to the timely implementation of revised charge rates, limited evidence of formal three-year cost recovery monitoring and an absence of recent statutory financial statements.

findings.headline: Procurement card controls failed to recover approximately £25k in VAT during 2025/26
findings.detail: Auditors found that cardholders systematically failed to retain valid VAT receipts, resulting in unrecovered VAT on expenditure. Annual reporting identified almost £25k of unrecovered VAT during 2025/26, largely on bed and breakfast accommodation. Testing alone estimated £14k over a five-month period, showing the scale of the leak.
findings.matters: This is a quantifiable cash loss from a control failure in a high-volume transaction process, indicating expenditure approval and documentation controls are not operating effectively.
findings.figures: £25k unrecovered VAT in 2025/26; approximately £14k over a five-month testing period
findings.quote: Testing estimated approximately £14k of unrecovered VAT over a five-month period, while annual reporting identified almost £25k of unrecovered VAT during 2025/26, largely relating to bed and breakfast accommodation costs.

findings.headline: Artificial Intelligence audit received only Reasonable Assurance, the weakest rating in this period
findings.detail: Of seven completed audits, only the Artificial Intelligence audit received Reasonable Assurance—meaning basic controls are in place but improvements are required. The other six audits all received Full or Substantial Assurance. Reasonable Assurance indicates the control environment is weaker for AI than across the council's established functions.
findings.matters: AI governance is an emerging risk area where councils' control maturity is variable; this council's weaker assurance on AI suggests governance development is incomplete in this domain.
findings.figures: 1 audit with Reasonable Assurance; 6 audits with Full or Substantial Assurance
findings.quote: For this period of work there was one audit report issued that gave a Reasonable assurance – Artificial Intelligence.

findings.headline: Five significant or fundamental audit recommendations remain overdue
findings.detail: The council still has 5 overdue significant and fundamental audit recommendations as of mid-September 2026, down from 11 at the previous reporting point. This means control weaknesses identified by audit remain unfixed and the risk exposure from these gaps continues.
findings.matters: Overdue audit recommendations indicate control weaknesses are not being remediated; extended delays to fix identified gaps leave the council operating with known vulnerabilities.
findings.figures: 5 overdue recommendations (previously 11)
findings.quote: Appendix 1 shows all overdue fundamental & significant recommendations at the time of this report, 5 recommendations (previously 11) in total.

findings.headline: Council holds £110.1M usable reserves and no external borrowing, providing substantial financial resilience
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the council has usable reserves of £110.1M, with General Fund Balance of £1.5M and risk reserves of £19.6M (excluding Business Rates Risk Reserve). The CFO confirmed 'large property and investment portfolios and no external borrowing'. The S151 Officer notes 'significant headroom' to absorb inflationary or cost pressures and access to external borrowing if needed.
findings.matters: A lender considers reserve adequacy a key credit indicator. The council's substantial reserve position and absence of external debt provide significant buffer against adverse events and indicate financial prudence, though the LGR event could affect sustainability of these reserves if reorganisation costs are material.
findings.figures: £110.1M usable reserves; £1.5M General Fund Balance; £19.6M risk reserves (excluding Business Rates Risk Reserve); £21.2M cash and cash equivalents; £46.6M long-term strategic investments
findings.quote: The council has usable reserves of £110.1M as at 31 March 2026...large property and investment portfolios and no external borrowing.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for 1 April 2028 will create new unitary authority covering Basingstoke and Deane, Hart and Rushmoor
findings.detail: Following Secretary of State decision on 25 March 2026, the council will be reorganised as part of new unitary authority structure across Hampshire. Elections to new authorities are scheduled May 2027, with new authorities taking over services from 1 April 2028. The council has flagged this as a Medium (Possible, Critical impact) strategic risk requiring significant preparation and resources.
findings.matters: A lender assesses governance stability and continuity of management. Fundamental local government reorganisation creates uncertainty around service delivery, management capability, and borrowing arrangements during transition, particularly if reorganisation consumes management attention and resources.
findings.figures: Elections scheduled May 2027; new authorities take over 1 April 2028; risk register assesses as Medium Possible Critical
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation across Hampshire is expected to replace the existing mainland councils with new unitary councils from 1 April 2028.

findings.headline: Manydown Garden Communities joint venture recorded £2.5M loss in 2025/26, the council's share of a £5.0M partnership loss
findings.detail: The council holds a 50% interest in MGC LLP, a housing development joint venture with Hampshire County Council and private sector partner Urban & Civic. MGC reported a loss of £5.0M for year ending 31 December 2025, of which the council's share is £2.5M. The council's share of net assets is £20.6M. The partnership remains asset-heavy (£71.0M land inventory) with £29.7M debt owed to Urban & Civic.
findings.matters: This represents a material investment (£20.6M net assets) in a loss-making venture. A lender would want to understand the trajectory of this investment and whether further losses or capital calls could impact the council's reserves.
findings.figures: Council's £2.5M share of £5.0M partnership loss; £20.6M council's share of net assets; £71.0M land inventory in partnership; £29.7M debt owed to development partner
findings.quote: As at 31 December 2025, Manydown Garden Communities LLP reported net assets of £41.3M and a loss of £5.0M for the year...The councils' share of the net assets is £20.6M, and their share of the loss for the year is £2.5M.

findings.headline: Investment property rental income of £19.1M is almost double council tax income and essential to service delivery
findings.detail: The council's property portfolio generated net rental income of approximately £19.1M during 2025/26, compared to £10.3M council tax income. The CFO states this is 'fundamental to its ability to continue to deliver front line services'. This represents high income concentration risk and dependency on property market conditions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's income diversification and vulnerability to property market shocks. If property values fell significantly or rental income declined, the council would face acute budget pressures without alternative income sources of similar scale.
findings.figures: £19.1M investment property rental income; £10.3M council tax income; property portfolio is 'almost double' the council tax revenue
findings.quote: its property portfolio continued to generate net rental income of around £19.1M during 2025/26. This is almost double the income the council receives from council tax and is fundamental to its ability to continue to deliver front line services that its residents value.

findings.headline: Council achieved £1.51M revenue outturn surplus in 2025/26
findings.detail: Against an originally balanced budget, the council reported a final surplus after carry-forwards. This surplus was transferred to reserves: £0.58M to Budget Carry Forward Reserve and £0.93M to MTFS Risk Reserve. This represents effective budget management and financial control during a year of cost pressures.
findings.matters: A lender would want to see the council not only balancing its budget but achieving surplus despite continuing cost and demand pressures, demonstrating financial discipline.
findings.figures: £1.51M outturn surplus; £1.47M net underspend on services cost; positive variances across multiple income lines including £1.23M on Interest and Investment Income
findings.quote: The net revenue expenditure outturn variance, after carry forwards of grants to reserves, was a final surplus of £1.51M.

findings.headline: Investment property valuation remains subject to query and holds material balance-sheet risk
findings.detail: Investment property represents £298m on the balance sheet but one valuation query remains outstanding relating to indexation presentation, with a separate unadjusted £0.3m difference on Fanum House reflecting 'a judgemental difference in valuation assumptions'. Auditor procedures on valuation are 'subject to final executive review'.
findings.matters: Investment property is 40% of assets on the balance sheet; ongoing valuation queries reflect estimation uncertainty on a material and illiquid asset class; resolution will affect reported net worth.
findings.figures: Investment Property balance: £298m; Fanum House unadjusted difference: £320k; Investment Property PPE additions: £10.5m
findings.quote: There was one unadjusted audit difference relating to Fanum House of £320k. This is outlined in Section 05.

findings.headline: Errors in NDR appeals provision spreadsheet required correction; management committing to enhanced control processes
findings.detail: The auditor identified errors in the spreadsheet used to calculate the NDR Appeals Provision which resulted in the provision being understated; management corrected it in the draft accounts. The auditor has recommended implementation of 'a formal review and sign-off process for key financial models and spreadsheets, including checks of formulas and data inputs' and the Chief Financial Officer has committed to this before financial statements preparation.
findings.matters: Errors in core financial calculations suggest gaps in quality assurance over financial reporting; while this specific error was caught in audit, indicates ongoing risk of misstatement in other key areas.
findings.figures: NDR appeals provision error corrected; materiality threshold £0.13m
findings.quote: We identified errors in the spreadsheet used to calculate the NDR Appeals Provision, which resulted in the provision being understated. The calculation was corrected by management and the financial statements were updated accordingly.

findings.headline: Two uncorrected audit differences totalling £0.5m reflect valuation disputes on pensions and investment property
findings.detail: Management has not corrected two judgemental audit differences: a £0.2m variance on pension liability arising from the Goodwin case, and a £0.3m overstatement of investment property value for Fanum House. The auditor explicitly states 'There are two uncorrected audit differences – one related to Investment Property and the other related to Pensions' and has asked the Audit Committee to confirm management's rationale for not adjusting them.
findings.matters: Persistent disagreement with management on valuation of material balance-sheet items signals either asset quality issues or inconsistent application of accounting standards; these affect both net asset position and reported reserves.
findings.figures: £0.2m pension liability (Goodwin case); £0.3m investment property (Fanum House valuation); total £0.5m unadjusted
findings.quote: There are two uncorrected audit differences – one related to Investment Property and the other related to Pensions

findings.headline: Scope of expected qualified opinion still undetermined as reserves rebuild work continues
findings.detail: The Council is expected to receive a qualified audit opinion, but the auditor has not yet concluded which areas the qualification will cover. Procedures to rebuild assurance over reserves from prior disclaimer periods remain in progress, with the status of General Fund Balance, Revaluation Reserve, Capital Adjustment Account, and Pooled Investments Fund marked as 'to be confirmed' rather than full or partial assurance. The auditor notes that 'the basis and scope of that qualification will be determined upon completion of the remaining audit procedures'.
findings.matters: A year into financial recovery, the Council cannot yet advise what audit limitations will apply to this year's statements or how material the reserves position remains uncertain; reserves are essential to financial resilience and a lender's assessment of capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: Reserves rebuild status: General Fund Balance, Revaluation Reserve, Capital Adjustment Account, Pooled Investments Fund all marked TBC; rebuild work commissioned under MHCLG audit recovery programme
findings.quote: Although a qualification is anticipated, the basis and scope of that qualification will be determined upon completion of the remaining audit procedures.

findings.headline: Monitoring of AI usage and compliance is ad-hoc rather than formalised, creating blind spots in detecting non-compliance and emerging risks.
findings.detail: The audit found that monitoring arrangements are developing rather than embedded. IT has undertaken some activity reporting (including on ChatGPT use), but there is no formalised ongoing monitoring process defining what will be monitored, how exceptions will be followed up, or how information will be reported to governance groups. This audit's use of ChatGPT monitoring data to target questionnaire follow-up demonstrated monitoring value but also highlighted that it is currently reactive rather than routine.
findings.matters: Without formalised, routine monitoring of AI tool compliance, the council cannot be assured that policy requirements are being consistently followed; operational risks and non-compliance incidents may go undetected until identified by audit or incident.
findings.figures: No figures on monitoring coverage or detected non-compliance incidents
findings.quote: there is not yet a formalised ongoing monitoring process setting out what AI usage will be monitored, how exceptions will be followed up, how information will be reported to governance groups or how learning from monitoring will be used to improve guidance & training

findings.headline: Thirteen audit recommendations issued, most categorised as Significant risk, indicating multiple material control gaps in the council's AI governance framework.
findings.detail: The audit identified control weaknesses spanning governance ownership, practical guidance for staff, embedding AI risks into service risk registers, disclosure and accountability expectations, human oversight reinforcement, approved tools clarity, approval and assurance processes, procurement integration, training programmes, member expectations, and formalised monitoring. Management has agreed all recommendations but most require substantial work to implement.
findings.matters: The breadth and severity of audit findings indicate the council's AI governance structure, while conceptually sound, has material gaps in implementation; multiple Significant-rated recommendations suggest the control environment is not yet fully effective.
findings.figures: 13 recommendations issued; majority categorised as Significant or Fundamental risk; completion timescales range from December 2026 to March 2027
findings.quote: arrangements remain at an early development stage and further work is required to embed governance responsibilities, provide more practical guidance, strengthen monitoring and ensure AI risks are managed consistently as use of the technology increases across services

findings.headline: AI policy controls exist but are not yet embedded in operational practice, with staff compliance and understanding incomplete.
findings.detail: The council has established an AI policy with clear restrictions and approval requirements. However, practical application remains developing. While 75% of staff have read the policy, 21% are unaware or unsure about DPIA requirements, and 15% either reported using non-public information in AI tools or were unsure whether they had done so. Some staff used unapproved AI tools without seeking required approval.
findings.matters: A finance director assessing control effectiveness must distinguish between policies on paper and controls actually working; operational staff uncertainty about compliance indicates the control framework is fragile and not yet delivering consistent adherence.
findings.figures: 75% of staff read the policy; 21% unaware or unsure about DPIA requirements; 15% reported using or unsure about using non-public information in AI tools; 79% of staff aware that DPIA may be required
findings.quote: the policy has not yet been fully embedded in practical terms, with requests for clearer 'do's and don'ts' guidance, examples/templates, training sessions, ongoing policy updates & clearer approval routes

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is creating emerging cost pressures and profound budget uncertainty beyond 2028
findings.detail: The council has already spent £0.12M preparing for potential local government reorganisation across Hampshire. The report explicitly states that while 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets are balanced, uncertainty exists beyond 2028 due to unknown transition costs. This represents an unquantified and potentially material future liability.
findings.matters: Reorganisation could fundamentally reshape the council's cost structure and revenue base. The council cannot predict future-year budgets, and transition costs could require significant reserve drawdowns or service reductions.
findings.figures: £0.12M already spent on reorganisation preparation; unknown costs beyond 2027/28
findings.quote: Whilst the 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets are balanced; uncertainty still exists for the following years given current global economic uncertainty and the developing transition costs relating to local government reorganisation across Hampshire.

findings.headline: Savings delivery is falling short; only 70% of targets achieved due to competing resilience needs
findings.detail: The council achieved only £1.95M of £2.79M planned savings and pressures (70% achievement). Specifically, £0.08M of savings from service and management reviews could not be delivered because the council had to invest in resilience—emergency planning, business continuity, and programme management capacity—particularly ahead of local government reorganisation. This suggests competing pressures on the budget.
findings.matters: Underperformance on savings targets, combined with emerging reorganisation costs, indicates the budget is structurally tighter than planned. Future years may struggle to balance if savings cannot be found.
findings.figures: £0.84M of planned savings not achieved (70% achievement rate); £0.08M specifically unachieved from service reviews
findings.quote: While reviews have resulted in streamlined reporting as anticipated, there has been a need to improve resilience in areas including emergency planning, business continuity and programme management, particularly ahead of Local Government Reorganisation. As a result, the council has not fully achieved this saving.

findings.headline: Waste contract costs have overrun budget; recovery depends on one-time Extended Producer Responsibility income
findings.detail: The new waste contract cost £0.30M more than budgeted because vehicle configurations for the food waste fleet differed from assumptions. The council absorbed this partly through a £1.09M Extended Producer Responsibility income windfall, which is now being used to replenish reserves that have been drawn down to cover waste overspends in prior years. This is not a sustainable fix.
findings.matters: Major contracts are proving difficult to forecast, forcing the council to rely on reserves. If EPR income drops or the waste contract costs continue to rise, this becomes a structural budget problem.
findings.figures: £0.30M contract overspend; £1.09M EPR income recovery; reserves historically drawn to cover waste costs
findings.quote: There is a overspend of £0.30M due to the actual costs associated with the new waste contract. This resulted from changed vehicle configurations for the stand-alone food waste fleet that were not known at the time of budget setting.

findings.headline: Local Plan has been delayed due to significant infrastructure constraints, affecting growth capacity
findings.detail: Stakeholders identified major infrastructure constraints during the regulation 18 consultation that now require substantial rework of the draft Local Plan. This pushed the schedule back and requires carrying forward £0.34M of budget. The constraints suggest the borough faces capacity limits that could restrict development and planning-related income.
findings.matters: A constrained Local Plan limits the council's development strategy and future fee income from planning applications. It also signals infrastructure bottlenecks that could affect economic resilience and the borough's attractiveness to investors.
findings.figures: £0.34M budget carry forward required due to plan-making delays
findings.quote: Due to significant infrastructure constraints identified by stakeholder organisations through the regulation 18 consultation on the draft Plan, further work is now required to determine the way forward for plan making in the immediate term.

findings.headline: Housing Benefits overspend from Universal Credit migration is structural and ongoing
findings.detail: The council overspent by £0.61M on Housing Benefits because as cases migrate to Universal Credit, the council pays administrative costs it cannot recover from government subsidy. Rent rebates also cost more while subsidy has reduced. This is not a one-off event but a structural issue that will persist as rollout continues.
findings.matters: Housing Benefits costs are now systematically higher than the government's subsidy model provides. This creates an ongoing deficit that will recur annually and may require either service cuts or budget reallocation to fund.
findings.figures: £0.61M adverse variance in 2025/26; ongoing impact to budget sustainability
findings.quote: The migration to Universal credit is primarily cases with full subsidy, meaning the council incurs more cost than it recovers on remaining cases. The cost to the council of rent rebates has also increased, with greater cost and reduced subsidy in that area also.

findings.headline: Portfolio rebalanced toward liquidity to fund capital expenditure, reducing long-term investments from prior years.
findings.detail: The treasury team deliberately reduced the proportion of long-term investments from prior levels to ensure cash is available for the council's forthcoming capital expenditure. Short-term and liquidity investments now comprise 61% of the portfolio (up from historical patterns). The council still holds £44.3M in long-term investments but has significantly increased its ability to deploy cash in the near term.
findings.matters: The shift indicates capital expenditure plans are pressing or significant. A lender would want to understand the scale and timing of planned capital spending, which is not detailed in this report.
findings.figures: 61% short-term/liquidity investments vs 39% long-term; long-term investments include £10M new local authority loans plus £18.9M gilts and £10M supranational bonds
findings.quote: The proportion of long-term investments has reduced, compared to previous years, in order to ensure funds are available for the council's forthcoming capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation: Basingstoke and Deane will merge with Hart and Rushmoor councils effective 1 April 2028.
findings.detail: On 25 March 2026, MHCLG approved the merger proposal. The council is proposing amendments to treasury strategy limits to exclude loans to Hart or Rushmoor from the individual £10M counterparty limit (allowing individual loans to exceed £10M), and to increase the 'Prudential Limit for Long-Term Principal Investments to Mature' from £20M to £50M in 2027/28 and 2028/29. These changes facilitate new lending to the merging councils but are expressly time-limited — loans would not extend beyond April 2028.
findings.matters: A lender would want visibility of major structural changes to the council's operations and financial management. Mergers carry execution risk, and the council's treasury capacity will be absorbed into a larger authority from April 2028.
findings.figures: Merger effective 1 April 2028; proposed limit increase from £20M to £50M for years 2027/28 and 2028/29 only
findings.quote: On 25 March 2026 the MHCLG approved proposals for Basingstoke and Deane, Hart and Rushmoor councils to merge as part of the Local Government Reorganisation effective on 1st April 2028.

findings.headline: Sharp increase in lending to other local authorities: £40M total, predominantly multi-year fixed-rate loans to councils across England.
findings.detail: The council made £10M in new long-term loans to local authorities (Northumberland £10M at 4.30% to October 2027; Central Bedfordshire £5M at 5.50% to June 2026; others) and maintained £30M in short-term rolling loans. This is a new exposure: there were zero long-term loans to other councils at the start of 2025/26. Loans span seven councils: Basildon, Central Bedfordshire, Dorset, Gravesham, Northumberland, and Suffolk. All are at fixed rates of interest.
findings.matters: Lending to distressed local authorities carries credit risk if the sector faces stress. The council is now materially exposed to other councils' financial performance. All target councils are facing similar budget pressures to Basingstoke itself.
findings.figures: £40M total in local authority loans (35% of total investments); long-term loans grew from £0M to £10M; short-term loans remain at £30M rolling
findings.quote: Short-term investments are comprised of loans to other local authorities at fixed rates of interest... Investments held at fixed rates of interest made up 60% of the total held on 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Unrealised losses on pooled investment funds of £2.36M, though protected from accounts impact until 2029/30 by statutory override.
findings.detail: The council holds £25M in bond and property funds (Royal London credit fund and CCLA property fund) with a marked-to-market valuation of £22.64M as of 31 March 2026, representing a £2.36M unrealised loss since purchase. The funds recovered slightly during the year (up £0.03M) but remain underwater. MHCLG's IFRS 9 statutory override means valuation changes will not affect the council's income and expenditure account until at least 2029/30, providing time for recovery or orderly disposal.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether the council has flexibility to hold these funds until recovery or faces pressure to realise losses. The statutory protection is temporary and runs only to 2029/30.
findings.figures: £22.64M valuation vs £25.00M cost = £2.36M unrealised loss; funds increased £0.03M in 2025/26
findings.quote: On 31 March 2026 the valuation of the council's externally managed funds was £22.64M compared to an initial cost of £25.00M, therefore showing a reduction of £2.36M since purchase.

findings.headline: Manydown joint venture loan drawdowns are unpredictable and dependent on an external partner's cashflow
findings.detail: The council is providing on-demand loan funding to Manydown Garden Communities LLP (a joint venture with Hampshire County Council). In 2025-26, a £0.090M loan was not drawn despite being budgeted, because the LLP's supplier invoices arrived later than expected. The timing is entirely outside the council's control and driven by 'third-party supplier invoicing'.
findings.matters: On-demand loan facilities to external partners create uncertainty in the council's own cashflow forecasting and could force the council to hold excess cash or delay other capital spend. The £1.750M Manydown internal borrowing (B Loan Note) shown in Table 10 is therefore exposed to timing risk.
findings.figures: Manydown Development rephased spend: £0.132M in 2025-26 (predominantly £0.090M loan not drawn). Total Manydown internal borrowing to 2029-30: £1.750M.
findings.quote: The underspend predominantly (£0.090M) relates to the council providing on‑demand loan funding to Manydown Garden Communities LLP, a joint venture with Hampshire County Council (HCC). The timing of loan drawdowns is dependent on the LLP's cash flow requirements, which are driven by third‑party supplier invoicing.

findings.headline: Widespread delays and slippage across major schemes suggest project delivery challenges
findings.detail: In 2025-26 alone, ten schemes with budgets over £0.1M were rephased into future years, including the Basing View 5G Living Lab (£0.786M), ICT Replacement (£0.382M), community facilities (£0.275M), and council vehicles (£0.335M). Multiple schemes cite external factors — SSE wayleave agreement delays, superior landlord permissions, contractor availability, and weather — indicating limited control over timescales.
findings.matters: If the council consistently fails to deliver schemes on forecast timescales, either capital receipts will remain in cash longer than expected (tying up resources) or future years' programmes will slip, compressing the delivery window and creating further pressure.
findings.figures: Total 2025-26 rephased spend: £1.434M. Major items: Basing View 5G Living Lab £0.786M, ICT Replacement Programme £0.382M, Community Infrastructure Fund £0.275M, Replacement of Council Owned Vehicles £0.335M.
findings.quote: Due to some delays in securing final permissions from the superior landlord, and the need to align the network installation with the fit out of the space, the indoor network has been installed in May 2026, running final tests in June 2026.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast assumes £4M Manydown land sale and £4.5M property disposals — nearly 82% of expected new receipts
findings.detail: Of the £10.361M forecast new capital receipts, £4.0M comes from the Manydown land sale and £4.52M from property investment strategy disposals. The remaining £1.841M comes from vehicle loan repayments and equipment sales. The report notes that actual receipts can differ materially from forecast, particularly 'with regard to the value and timing of anticipated capital receipts'.
findings.matters: If the Manydown land sale is delayed or yields less than forecast, or if property disposals underperform, the council will lack headroom to deliver its capital programme or will need to increase borrowing. This creates liquidity risk.
findings.figures: Gross new capital receipts assumed: £10.361M (comprising Manydown land £4.000M, PIS disposals £4.520M, vehicle repayments £0.841M). This is 34% of total capital receipts planned across the revised programme (£42.480M of £121.704M).
findings.quote: This includes gross receipts of £4.000M in respect of the land at Manydown, property investment strategy disposals of £4.520M; loan repayments related to service-based loans e.g. new waste vehicles and sales of council owned vehicles as part of the rolling replacement programme of £0.841M and an anticipated partial receipt of £1.000M linked to the reprovision of the golf site.

findings.headline: A £59M leisure park redevelopment programme backed by £10.8M internal borrowing in 2029-30
findings.detail: The revised capital programme includes a £59.2M redevelopment of the leisure park spread across 2027-2030, with the council using internal borrowing to cover £10.781M in 2029-30 — equivalent to 18% of that scheme's budget. This relies on generating sufficient capital receipts over the next four years to fund the programme, with forecast new receipts of only £10.361M across 2026-29.
findings.matters: This level of internal borrowing signals tight cashflow and dependency on achieving forecast asset sales. If property receipts underperform, the council may struggle to deliver the leisure park scheme or need external borrowing.
findings.figures: Leisure Park Redevelopment: £59.216M total (£1.506M 2026-27, £23.400M 2027-28, £20.110M 2028-29, £14.200M 2029-30). Internal Borrowing for Leisure Park: £10.781M in 2029-30. Gross new capital receipts forecast: £10.361M across 2026-29.
findings.quote: Internal Borrowing - Redevelopment of the Leisure Park 0.000 0.000 0.000 10.781

findings.headline: £20.4M annual revenue income concentrated in single geographic area creates vulnerability to local economic shocks
findings.detail: The council's investment property portfolio, which generates critical revenue income, is concentrated with 'most of the assets situated in or around Basingstoke town centre'. This geographic concentration creates exposure to local economic downturns in retail, office, or industrial property markets.
findings.matters: High-concentration income streams are more volatile; local economic downturn (retail decline, office vacancy, industrial shrinkage) could materially impact council budget sustainability
findings.figures: £20.4M forecast annual rental income from £289.8M portfolio; concentration in Basingstoke town centre geography
findings.quote: The council owns a substantial commercial investment property portfolio valued at £289.8M as at 31 March 2025 which is forecast to deliver an annual rental income of £20.4M in 2026/27; principally comprising office, industrial, retail and leisure property investments leased on commercial terms to third party tenants. The portfolio is located within the borough with most of the assets situated in or around Basingstoke town centre.

findings.headline: Property acquisitions programme frozen until disposal proceeds available; timing uncertain due to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Section 1.8 states the council needs to ensure transactions occur in best market conditions and requires capital funding from disposals before acquisitions can proceed. The flow is described as fluctuating, with capital budget allocations needing adjustment accordingly. This constrains strategic flexibility.
findings.matters: Unpredictable timing of capital availability affects multi-year strategic planning and borrowing decisions; LGR creates external constraint over which council has limited control
findings.figures: £289.8M portfolio valuation; £1.32M in disposal proceeds mentioned as in pipeline
findings.quote: Due to various factors, including Local Government Reorganisation, there is a need to ensure such transactions occur in the best market conditions together with the required capital funding from disposals before acquisitions can occur. The flow of such transactions will fluctuate and the budget allocation within the capital programme will need to be adjusted accordingly.

findings.headline: Council flagging health and safety compliance deficiencies in property portfolio requiring additional resource investment
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that additional resources have been proposed to ensure the operational property portfolio meets health and safety requirements. The phrasing 'not putting the council at risk of prosecution' indicates existing gaps in compliance that are being remediated.
findings.matters: Property compliance failures create liability and reputational risk; additional spend required indicates past under-investment in maintenance or compliance standards
findings.figures: Additional resources proposed (specific amount not quantified)
findings.quote: Additional resources have been proposed to enable work to be progressed to ensure the property portfolio is not only fit for purpose, having good environmental credentials, attracting commercial rents where appropriate, but also meets health and safety requirements and not putting the council at risk of prosecution.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Revenue contributions to capital of £4.000M per annum are the planned funding mechanism for future years, constraining revenue budget flexibility
findings.detail: The paper states 'There will be greater reliability on the annual revenue contribution to capital included in the MTFS update – currently £4.000M per annum.' This means £4M of annual revenue budget (money that could fund services or build reserves) is being committed to capital, reducing the revenue budget's flexibility to respond to service demand or financial pressure.
findings.matters: A large revenue-to-capital contribution reduces the council's revenue budget flexibility and indicates it is relying on revenue cash to fund capital investment rather than genuine capital receipts or grants. This is structurally weaker than capital receipt-funded programmes.
findings.figures: £4.000M per annum revenue contribution to capital, forecast as 'greater reliance' in future years
findings.quote: In future years there will be greater reliability on the annual revenue contribution to capital included in the MTFS update – currently £4.000M per annum.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Capital programme grew £28.115M net despite scheme savings removals, driven by additions of £31.140M
findings.detail: The council added £31.140M in new capital schemes while removing only £3.025M in scheme savings, resulting in a net 27.8% increase to the capital programme from £101.161M to £129.276M. This is an aggressive capital expansion in an environment where internal borrowing is required and revenue contributions to capital are constrained at £4.000M per annum.
findings.matters: A large expansion in capital commitments at a time when liquidity is being drawn down (internal borrowing) and revenue budget is tight signals either optimism about future receipts or lack of capital constraint discipline. The council states it is 'fully funded from council resources up to 2029/30', but that funding includes reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Additions: £31.140M; Savings removed: £3.025M; Net increase: £28.115M; Programme growth: 27.8%
findings.quote: It is recommended that Council: 1. Agrees the addition of £31.140M to the capital programme and the removal of scheme underspends of £3.025M, which gives rise to a net increase of £28.115M to the overall capital programme

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Manydown development financing wholly dependent on future Homes England support, with council loan funding rephased into later years
findings.detail: The £1.020M Manydown rephasing is justified on the basis that 'The project will soon have the support of Homes England finance to fund infrastructure delivery. With interim B-Loan financing for infrastructure being provided by Urban & Civic and not the councils it is proposed to rephase the council's loan funding into future years.' The council is betting on external (government) finance arriving to reduce its own funding burden, creating dependency and timeline risk.
findings.matters: The council's participation in Manydown is conditional on Homes England finance materialising. If that funding is delayed or withdrawn, the council faces sudden capital demand or scheme delivery risk. The scheme is also funded via a B-Loan note (internal borrowing).
findings.figures: £1.020M rephased from 2025/26; £2.589M internal borrowing (B-Loan Note) allocated to Manydown
findings.quote: The project will soon have the support of Homes England finance to fund infrastructure delivery. With interim B-Loan financing for infrastructure being provided by Urban & Civic and not the councils it is proposed to rephase the council's loan funding into future years.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Property Investment Strategy stalling with £0.624M rephased because no suitable investment properties identified
findings.detail: The council's Property Investment Strategy, budgeted at £0.624M for 2025/26, has been entirely rephased into 2026/27 because 'no suitable properties being identified in the market'. This is a strategic pause on property acquisition, signalling either market conditions are unfavourable or the council lacks investment capacity.
findings.matters: Property investment is typically part of a council's income diversification strategy. A pause in acquisitions may indicate either market constraint or that the council is prioritising cash preservation over income generation.
findings.figures: £0.624M rephased from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.quote: It is unlikely an investment property acquisition will now take place in 2025/26 due no suitable properties being identified in the market. The request is therefore to rephase the £0.624M funded from property capital receipts achieved under the property investment strategy.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Low Cost Home Ownership scheme underperforming with housing market pressure limiting uptake
findings.detail: The council's Own Home Loan scheme is experiencing lower-than-expected take-up. The paper states interest 'has not always materialised into property purchases. This can mostly be attributed to pressures in the housing market.' Only 7 loans are forecast to complete in 2025/26, requiring £0.162M of remaining budget to be rephased into 2026/27. This signals the council's housing growth strategy is stalling.
findings.matters: The scheme's underperformance reflects housing market weakness and suggests the council's assumptions about housing demand and development are not being met. This affects the credibility of any growth-based financial projections.
findings.figures: Only 7 loans forecast for 2025/26 (implying significantly fewer than originally planned); £0.162M rephased from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.quote: Whilst the Own Home Loan scheme is in popular demand the interest has not always materialised into property purchases. This can mostly be attributed to pressures in the housing market. It is expected there will be fewer completions than originally anticipated in 2025/26, with the forecast being for seven loans to complete in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Basing View Car Parks moving to reactive maintenance after £2.05M capital budget removed
findings.detail: The council removed £2.050M of planned capital spend on Basing View car parks (including Fanum House and Plot K). The rationale is that a 'more detailed review has established that a reactive approach to maintenance will be adopted' pending future regeneration plans. This is a deliberate downgrade from planned capital maintenance to reactive spend, a cash preservation move that increases future failure risk.
findings.matters: Switching from planned maintenance to reactive maintenance is typically a short-term cash preservation move that generates higher long-term costs and service failure risk. It signals capital constraint and suggests other assets may face the same downgrade.
findings.figures: £2.050M removed (£0.275M in 2025/26, £1.475M in 2026/27, £0.300M in 2027/28); £0.850M saving in 2026/27 via 'revised plan for Plot K car park' with 'lower-cost approach'
findings.quote: A more detailed review of Fanum House has established that a reactive approach to maintenance will be adopted in the car park with minimum capital works required until the regeneration plans of the entire site is clearer. This would negate the rationale for capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Eastland's car park smoke extraction system is non-operational and requires immediate capital investment despite identified as legal/fire safety requirement
findings.detail: The Property Investment Strategy adds £0.050M in 2026/27 for installation of a smoke extraction system in Eastland's car park basement. The paper notes the existing system is 'non-operational' and states this 'has been identified as a legal requirement and forms part of the original fire safety strategy'. This is a compliance-driven, non-discretionary capital need that should have been identified earlier.
findings.matters: A non-operational fire safety system is a compliance gap. The fact that this has only now entered the capital plan (rather than being an emergency repair) suggests gaps in asset condition monitoring or regulatory compliance tracking.
findings.figures: £0.050M in 2026/27 and £0.450M (for other works at Eastlands)
findings.quote: An additional £0.050M in 2026/27 and £0.450M in 2026/27 is requested to install a smoke extraction system in the basement of Eastland's car park as the existing one is non-operational. This system has been identified as a legal requirement

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Malls shopping centre car park requires £2.7M in structural remedial works due to water ingress from cracks
findings.detail: The council's Property Investment Strategy includes £1.400M in 2026/27 and £1.300M in 2027/28 for Malls car park resurfacing. The paper explicitly states this is needed because 'cracks in the existing surface have resulted in ongoing maintenance problems' and water ingress into units below. This is reactive maintenance on a commercial property, indicating deferred capital maintenance and portfolio stress.
findings.matters: Structural defects requiring £2.7M in immediate works signal an ageing asset portfolio and possible underinvestment. The council is a property owner generating commercial income; water ingress affecting commercial tenants creates liability and rent-collection risk.
findings.figures: £1.400M in 2026/27; £1.300M in 2027/28; total £2.700M over two years
findings.quote: It is proposed to increase the capital scheme by £1.400M in 2026/27 and £1.300M in 2027/28 to fund resurfacing works for the car park at The Malls shopping centre. The project will ensure the car park remains safe and fit for purpose while addressing structural issues that have led to water ingress into the units below.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Leisure Park redevelopment experiencing significant schedule slippage on a £60M+ scheme
findings.detail: The scheme was originally approved for £35.368M by 2027/28 but bidders' programmes now indicate design and planning only in 2026/27, with construction not commencing until 2027/28. A further £14.200M is being added as 'balance of the original approved sum', bringing the total commitment forward. This two-year delay on a major scheme funded via internal borrowing creates execution and cost risk.
findings.matters: Major capital projects with schedule delays typically face cost inflation and carry delivery risk. For a lender, this signals either optimism bias in planning or constraints in the council's project delivery capacity. The scheme is a significant part of the capital programme (approximately 11% of total).
findings.figures: Total project £60M+ (£35.368M to 2027/28, £24.632M later years); £14.200M addition in this update; construction start delayed from 2026/27 to 2027/28
findings.quote: The bidders' indicative programme for this project are suggestive that the activity during 2026/27 will consist of design and planning work. The proposals indicate that the construction will not commence until 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update and Strategy Report for 202526 to 202930
findings.headline: Internal borrowing of £12.249M reduces cash liquidity and signals insufficient capital receipts
findings.detail: The council is using internal borrowing (cash reserves) to fund two major schemes: Manydown (£2.589M) and Leisure Park redevelopment (£9.660M). Total internal borrowing to 31/03/2030 is forecast at £13.697M. This depletes working capital and creates refinancing dependency on future capital receipts and Manydown loan repayments.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see the council maintaining adequate liquidity buffers. Using cash reserves for capital investment signals capital receipts are insufficient to fund the programme and reduces the council's ability to manage unexpected shortfalls or emergencies.
findings.figures: £12.249M internal borrowing 2025/26–2029/30; £13.697M cumulative to 31/03/2030; forecast replenishment from Manydown only by 2031/32
findings.quote: After financing the proposed capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30 which includes the use of revenue contributions to capital allowed for in the Medium Term Financial Strategy and £12.249M of internal borrowing

findings.headline: £302M commercial property portfolio acknowledged as illiquid and difficult to convert to cash quickly
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges property is 'comparatively difficult to sell and convert to cash at short notice and can take a considerable period to sell in certain market conditions,' relying on separate liquid cash reserves to cover this gap.
findings.matters: Liquidity risk: if council faces urgent cash need, the £300M+ majority of non-treasury assets cannot be quickly realized despite representing substantial portion of council resources.
findings.figures: £302M commercial property portfolio; council maintains liquid treasury reserves as offset
findings.quote: Compared with other investment types, property is comparatively difficult to sell and convert to cash at short notice and can take a considerable period to sell in certain market conditions.

findings.headline: No formal monitoring and reporting process exists for £3.03M in service-based loans
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states there is 'currently no formal monitoring and reporting of the service-based investments.' These loans (£2.30M to Sentinel Housing Association, £0.31M to SERCO) support council priority services including homelessness prevention and waste management.
findings.matters: Governance gap: without formal monitoring, the council cannot regularly assess credit quality, service delivery impact, or performance of major loans supporting critical services.
findings.figures: Total service-based loans £3.03M as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: There is currently no formal monitoring and reporting of the service-based investments.

findings.headline: Returns on Manydown loan notes declined sharply following 2024/25 land acquisition
findings.detail: Expected returns on Manydown loan notes fell from 11.59% (2024/25 actual) to 7.15% (2025/26 forecast) to 7.89% (2026/27 forecast). The strategy attributes this to changes in 'loan arrangements and terms following the land acquisition.'
findings.matters: A major recent investment is underperforming initial expectations, reducing forecast investment income and signalling execution risk on new investment activity.
findings.figures: Manydown loan notes: 11.59% (2024/25 actual) → 7.15% (2025/26 forecast) → 7.89% (2026/27 forecast)
findings.quote: The reduction in respect of the Manydown loan notes reflects the composition of loan arrangements and terms following the land acquisition which took place during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Council's service delivery cost base depends significantly on income from £334M investment portfolio
findings.detail: The strategy states that investment income is 'significant to the council and supports the cost of services.' With £334M exposed and average returns of 6.85% for 2026-27, this represents material operating income dependency with limited alternative sources.
findings.matters: Lender and finance director need to understand income volatility risk: if investment returns fall due to vacancy, capital loss, or market downturn, the council faces budget pressure with limited flexibility to replace this income.
findings.figures: Total non-treasury investment exposure £334M (forecast 31/03/2027); expected rate of return 6.85% for 2026-27
findings.quote: The income generated from non-treasury investments is significant to the council and supports the cost of services.

findings.headline: Government now actively discourages commercial property holdings by councils and restricts PWLB borrowing for this purpose
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges that policy has shifted: commercial property holdings by councils are 'actively discouraged, with restrictions put in place accessing PWLB borrowing for this purpose.' This is reinforced by CIPFA's Prudential Code provisions prohibiting borrowing primarily for income yield.
findings.matters: Policy risk to the council's existing model: government restrictions could limit the council's ability to refinance, restructure, or expand this portfolio, and may signal intention to further constrain local authority commercial investment.
findings.figures: £302.10M commercial property portfolio now operating in a policy environment that actively discourages this asset class
findings.quote: The holding of commercial properties by councils is now actively discouraged, with restrictions put in place accessing PWLB borrowing for this purpose, and by the explicit provisions of CIPFA's Prudential Code which prohibit borrowing primarily for income yield.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio of £302M is substantially larger than other district councils
findings.detail: The council holds £302.10M in investment property (as at 31 March 2025) and acknowledges it has a 'vastly different property portfolio compared to most other councils.' The scale requires a dedicated Property Services function and significant professional management.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand material asset concentration, the council's ability to manage this complexity, and the sustainability of this model relative to peers.
findings.figures: £302.10M in investment property as at 31/03/2025; total non-treasury investment exposure £334M forecast for 2026-27
findings.quote: Due to the size of its commercial property holdings, Basingstoke and Deane has a vastly different property portfolio compared to most other councils.

findings.headline: Major income dependency beyond planning horizon: Manydown development expected to deliver significant income after 2030
findings.detail: The Cabinet Member noted that 'significant income from the Manydown project was expected after 2030.' This development sits outside the current Medium-Term Financial Strategy and prudential planning period (to 2029/30), placing material future revenue dependency on a project not yet fully detailed in the current strategy.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand whether long-term financial sustainability assumes Manydown income and what risks exist if the project is delayed, costs more than expected, or generates lower returns.
findings.figures: Income timing: after 2030
findings.quote: The Cabinet Member for Finance and Property stated that significant income from the Manydown project was expected after 2030.

findings.headline: Property portfolio concentration: property is larger proportion of investments than treasury management, with gap between planned capex and property sales
findings.detail: The Audit Committee noted the council has planned expenditure of £11.6M on operational buildings while forecasting only £7.1M in property sales. The CFO confirmed 'property made up a larger proportion of the council's investments, but that the return from investment property was also greater.' This concentration in property and the £4.5M funding gap indicates reliance on either reserves or borrowing.
findings.matters: Concentration in property increases vulnerability to asset value and rental income shocks. The funding gap suggests the council cannot self-fund its capital programme through asset sales alone and depends on reserves or borrowing.
findings.figures: £11.6M planned operational buildings spending, £7.1M property sales forecast
findings.quote: The Chief Finance Officer confirmed that property made up a larger proportion of the council's investments, but that the return from investment property was also greater. Awareness was raised of planned expenditure of approximately £11.6M on operational buildings alongside a forecast of £7.1M for sales of property.

findings.headline: Investment income is critical to the council's ability to deliver services, indicating budget dependency on commercial returns
findings.detail: The report states that the investment strategy sets out 'the overall investment strategy for achieving the additional investment income targets set out in the budget report (property rents and interest) that is critical in providing the council with the resources necessary to deliver its priorities.' This makes clear the council's general fund depends on investment returns to fund ongoing service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender must understand that the council's operational budget is not self-sustaining and relies on property rental income and investment returns. Deterioration in property values or rental demand creates direct pressure on service budgets.
findings.figures: Not quantified in covering report
findings.quote: it sets out the overall investment strategy for achieving the additional investment income targets set out in the budget report (property rents and interest) that is critical in providing the council with the resources necessary to deliver its priorities.

findings.headline: £60M Leisure Park redevelopment is largest capital commitment with CFO confirming budget control
findings.detail: The council has committed to a £60M redevelopment of the Leisure Park, which represents the most significant capital scheme affecting the council's investment requirements to 2030. The Audit Committee questioned whether the estimate would remain at £60M and the CFO confirmed 'the redevelopment was expected to remain within the estimated £60M cost alongside an expected positive return', though the facility's value cannot be assessed until completion.
findings.matters: A £60M capital scheme is substantial and represents a major commitment of resources. Any variance from this estimate affects borrowing requirements and financial sustainability. The confidence in cost control directly affects credit risk.
findings.figures: £60M estimated cost
findings.quote: The Chief Finance Officer stated that the redevelopment was expected to remain within the estimated £60M cost alongside an expected positive return.

findings.headline: Audit Committee requested clarity on liquid reserves strategy beyond 2030 amid forecast tightness
findings.detail: The Audit Committee formally requested written clarification from Cabinet and the S151 Officer on plans for liquid reserves beyond 2030. With investments forecast to fall to £34.09M by year 4 and the council's primary objective stated as security and liquidity, the committee's request signals concern about medium-term reserve sufficiency.
findings.matters: Committee concern about liquidity beyond 2030 suggests uncertainty about whether declining reserves will be adequate to meet the council's operational and contingency needs. This questions the sustainability of the capital spending plan driving the decline.
findings.figures: Forecast £34.09M investment balance in year 4 (2029/30); minimum liquidity target £15M maintained within money market funds
findings.quote: It was agreed that the Chair would write to the Cabinet and the Section 151 Officer to request consideration of the council's liquid reserves beyond 2030 and clarification of the plans in this area.

findings.headline: Audit Committee formally raised concern about potential imbalance between cash investments and commercial property investments
findings.detail: The committee questioned whether declining treasury investment balances are creating a misaligned risk profile given the council's concurrent property investment strategy. The committee requested that the chair write to Cabinet and the S151 Officer seeking clarification on future plans, suggesting the committee believes the overall investment strategy lacks balance.
findings.matters: Committee-level concerns about portfolio imbalance suggests debate over whether the council is taking on concentrated risk across cash and property assets. This is a governance red flag about strategic oversight of total investment risk.
findings.figures: Investment balances declining to £34.09M by year 4; property fund holdings currently £10M
findings.quote: The Committee questioned the reduction in the council's expected investment balances over the medium-term and suggested that there might be a potential imbalance between cash investments and commercial property investments.

findings.headline: Investment strategy rebalanced toward higher-risk local authority loans while Audit Committee flagged governance concerns
findings.detail: The council has increased its local authority loans limit from £40M to £50M while reducing bond funds from £40M to £30M. The Audit and Accounts Committee questioned this shift on 26 January 2026, specifically asking whether due diligence was being applied and whether counterparty limits should be tighter. The S151 Officer had to reassure the committee about 'appropriate due diligence' and 'reputational risks'.
findings.matters: Governance-level scrutiny of investment decisions signals internal uncertainty about risk management.
